lesson.title: Constant Rate of Change: Recognizing Linear Form
lesson.summary: Learn to recognize a linear form by its roughly constant rate of change, and see why real data can be linear without ever falling exactly on a line.
lesson.body:
A linear form is the special case of form of association where the points in a scatterplot cluster around what could be summarized by a single straight line. It does not require the points to fall exactly on a line, only that a straight line captures the overall trend reasonably well across the full range of the data, with points scattered somewhat above and below that imaginary line rather than curving systematically away from it.

Look again at the rate of change in the study hours and exam score data: from (1, 68) to (2, 72) the score rises 4 points, from (2, 72) to (3, 75) it rises 3 points, from (3, 75) to (4, 80) it rises 5 points, from (4, 80) to (5, 84) it rises 4 points, and from (5, 84) to (6, 90) it rises 6 points. None of those five increases are identical, yet they cluster fairly close to an average of about 4.4 points per additional hour, without any obvious pattern of speeding up or slowing down as hours increase. That rough constancy, increases hovering around the same value rather than systematically growing or shrinking, is what makes this data's form linear rather than curved.

It is important not to confuse a linear form with a perfect relationship. Real data almost never falls exactly on a line, there is nearly always some scatter caused by factors the explanatory variable does not capture, like differences in sleep, natural ability, or the difficulty of a particular exam question. A linear form simply means that scatter does not have a systematic curved shape to it. If you covered the exact numbers and just looked at the shape of the cloud, a straight line drawn through the middle would track the pattern about equally well on the left side and the right side, which is the visual test for linearity.

Recognizing a linear form is what justifies fitting a straight line, called a line of best fit, through the data later in this course, and it is also the exact condition under which the correlation coefficient, computed next, gives a meaningful summary of strength. Applying either of those tools to data that is not actually linear produces numbers that look precise but describe the wrong shape entirely, so confirming linear form is a required first step, not an optional formality.

For a sense of what a truly linear relationship looks like, consider converting temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit using F = 1.8C + 32. Every whole-degree increase in Celsius corresponds to exactly 1.8 degrees of increase in Fahrenheit, with zero scatter, since this is a mathematical formula rather than measured data. Plotting Celsius against Fahrenheit for any set of values produces points that fall exactly on a line. Real statistical data, like the study hours example, is never this exact, but it is judged linear whenever it approximates this constant-rate behavior closely enough that a straight line remains a fair summary.

Once you can recognize linear form by eye, the correlation coefficient gives you a way to put a number on exactly how tightly the points hug that imaginary line, turning the visual judgment you have been practicing into a precise, comparable statistic.
